read_from: The route text as served, in the extract this reissue counts (the serving lane's merge of 7 November 2026 AD: the route store's rows of this source followed by the span store's records of it; a span record is one JSON per line with key, route, def, m, year and cut, and the span store's own fields, which are not marks). The route store's rows: field 1 (the route text) of each row of reader/data/route-store of the main branch at commit 1d2470eb356b, store_version 3d8c4ef86c01 (its index.json; the store served on 7 November 2026 AD, 652,885 routes in all), for "Wikidata Hebrew lexeme explicit English sense gloss" (M87, M61, M2, M76, M94, M73, M81): 324 routes (axis: routes), byte for byte the 324 routes of the store of 31 October (commit 306f3b285898, store_version 87b13b1169b4) that the ledger of v136 read. The span store's records: the 29 records of this source in the span store as served (schema span-store-served-v1, from span-store-v2.1, dictionary store cc890b8a7992, ledgers applied on 2026-11-07; 1,698 records in all, axis: records), each a word or a phrase of two or more Hebrew words read as one, with its own route text, which the classifier reads like any route. Together 353 routes (axis: routes), 344 letters keys (axis: keys), 334 distinct route texts (axis: texts). The definition field of the same row equals the route text on 353 of the routes, and the store's cut flag stands on 0. The source audit of v136 covers the route store's rows: each such route's store record names lines of the lane's copy of the source (hebrew-english-glosses.jsonl, in ledgers/work/ldmprs/source-cache/wikidata-hebrew-lexemes-2026-07-14/, one answer of Wikidata's query service) with the word's sense id. The route text is the English text of that sense, the field skos:definition, on 324 of 324 of those routes, and every one of the 2,821 senses of that file has one English text. So such a route comes from one field, the text of one sense, and no test here stands on a guess about a field; the audit is evidence about the source and no part of any test. The span store's records were not audited against the source's file here; their texts are of the same kind (one English text of one sense), and the span store's own fields were not read for any test. The source's own key to its signs: none found. The lane holds 9 files of this source that are no answers (the queries, the manifests, the licence page, in that folder); the only words in them that name a sign stand in 2 of the lane's own manifests and speak of the spelling of the Hebrew form, not of the English. Of the 5 files of the lane's work on the works' own stamps that name Wikidata, none is Wikidata's own account of how a sense's text is written, as the script builder/05-key-search.mjs of v136 and its output source-audit/key-search.json show. A manifest names Wikidata's documentation of its query service by its address (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Lexicographical_data/Documentation/Query_Service); its body is not on file, and fetching it needs the owner's word. So every shape's meaning here begins "unverified:". What a sign does is read from the texts, and for the comma after a head word from the audit: 224 of the 315 senses behind the route store's routes name an item of Wikidata, and the English label and description of that item stand in hebrew-sense-item-english-fields.jsonl in the same folder.

definitions.terms: In every test a character is one Unicode code point (every route holds only characters of 16 bits, so a code point is one index of the JavaScript string). A letter is any character of Unicode category L (JavaScript \p{L}), of any script and in either case. A digit is one of 0 to 9, and no test asks for any other number character. A space is the character U+0020 only, and no test uses whitespace of any other kind. By name, a comma is «,», a slash is «/», and an opening round bracket is «(». Nothing is trimmed: the text is the whole route text as it stands, which is the field route of a line of the by-source JSONL, what the checker gives the classifier, and never the field def; the text before and the text after the mark are the template's c.before and c.after, and what a bracket holds is the template's c.group, the same for an opener and for its closer. Inside round brackets means that the template's c.container is the word paren. Directly before and directly after name the one character next to the mark or next to the named string; where the mark or the string stands at that end of the text no character stands there, so a test that asks for a character there fails, and a test that says no such character stands there holds. The whole text, exactly, means that the text equals the named string character for character. Begins with means that the first characters of the named thing are exactly the string, whatever follows them; it asks for no word end, and a space at the end of a string is part of the string. Holds means that the string stands somewhere in the named thing as a run of characters, whatever stands beside it; it asks for no word end. A string stands between « and », which are not part of it, and a full stop or comma after » belongs to the sentence and not to the string. Every string and every list minds case and is matched exact to the character.
definitions.first_match: For each mark the shapes are tried in the order they stand in this file; the first whose test holds names the occurrence, and no later shape is tried for it. Not caught above means that no earlier shape of the same mark took the occurrence. A shape's container field is not part of its test: a test looks at the container only where it says inside round brackets, and the checker compares the field afterwards.
definitions.pair_steps: These steps are the same for an opener and for its closer. The text before the pair: for an opener, the text before the mark; for a closer, the text before the mark with its last characters taken off, as many as what the bracket holds has, and one more for the opener.

homonyms.reason: The route text carries no entry number. The source gives each word (lexeme) an id and each sense of it an id (L7375, L7375-S1); the route store carries neither, and the dictionary store's record keeps them in its location field. So two texts under one letters key may be two senses of one word or senses of two words, and the route text cannot say which. A letters key here is the letters of one spelling of a word's lemma (this holds for 324 of 324 of the route store's routes by the audit, with final letters folded). By the audit, of the 8 keys of the route store's rows with more than one text (axis: keys; 315 letters keys among those rows), 8 are keys whose routes all come from one lexeme (example key ירק, whose 3 texts come from 1 lexeme), and 0 are keys whose routes come from two or more lexemes. The span store's records add 0 such keys among themselves and 0 keys whose texts stand one in the route store and one in the span store, not audited here; together 8 keys (axis: keys; 344 letters keys in all).

branches.question: Here the source gives each sense of a word one text, and some texts hold several words for that sense, with a comma or a slash between them: grief/mourning; trouble, disaster; nation, ethnic group. No sign in the row can tell whether one of the words means something different from the rest, and the line between a second word and a short description is a judgment, made row by row: Anas, genus of birds is not in this question. Today the page cuts at those commas, and it does not cut at the slashes. Should these signs cut the row? From the day this is wired, these rows print whole, at the commas too. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: Every one of these signs in these rows cuts: the page prints grief and mourning as two readings, and trouble and disaster as two, each word or wording as the source writes it.
No sign in these rows cuts: the page prints grief/mourning and trouble, disaster as one reading each, as written. At the commas this is a change from today.

branches.question: Some rows hold words with a slash between them that share a word or a phrase written only once. In to be exiled/deported the word deported means be deported; in pot used for cooking food by boiling/seething the word seething means a pot used for cooking food by seething. Alone, such a word says something else. Should the slash cut the row? Today the page prints each of these rows whole, and from the day this is wired it still does, unless you rule that it cuts. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: Every slash in these rows cuts: the page prints to be exiled and deported as two readings, and pot used for cooking food by boiling and seething as two. Each piece prints as the source writes it, without the words it shares, so deported stands alone where the source means to be deported, and seething where the source means a pot used for cooking food by seething.
No slash in these rows cuts: the page prints to be exiled/deported as one reading, as written, as it does today.

branches.question: Some rows hold two or more descriptions of the word, with a semicolon or a comma between them: ruby, variety of corundum, mineral, gemstone. The word at the head stands only before the first. Is each later description a further reading? Today the page cuts at those commas where the pieces are short and not at the semicolons; from the day this is wired, each of these rows prints without a cut there. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: Every one of these signs cuts: the page prints ruby, variety of corundum and mineral and gemstone as three readings. A later description prints without the word at the head, and with an or the source writes before it. The comma after the word at the head stays.
No sign in these rows cuts there: the page prints ruby, variety of corundum, mineral, gemstone as one reading, as written.

branches.question: Some rows hold only a note on a letter, a label or a description of a role, and no word that could stand in a verse: Hebrew letter, sounds like h or a; a given name, (first name). Should the page print them as readings? Today the page cuts these rows at the comma, except the row that opens either an item which provides, which it prints whole. From the day this is wired each prints as written, one reading. To leave them out the page needs one step of its own, because a declaration cannot leave a row out. This answer holds whatever you answer to the other questions.

options.means: The page prints each row as one reading, as written: Hebrew letter, sounds like h or a.
The page prints no pill for these rows, once it has the one step of its own that this answer needs; until then they print as written. They stay in the store as they are.

not_done_here: This ledger leaves to the store every route that holds no mark, because a shape stands only at a mark («male given name», «central figure of Christianity»); the rows it names for that question stand in rows-for-the-store-v1.jsonl, outside the shapes, as examples and no census from the route store's rows (the span store's records were not read for it), and nothing is struck. It leaves to the page the steps that the answers no_pill of B04 and name_alone of B05 ask for, since a declaration can cut a row and has no field that leaves a whole row out or a label out; no route divides at rest here. The span store's row that is only a note in a bracket («(posthumous honorific, "may the memory») is of B04's kind and stands outside B04, whose words about today's page do not hold for it; the serving lane may fold it under B04's answer.
